title: THE CHURCH CANNOT PREACH GRACE BY PRETENDING REPENTANCE IS UNNECESSARY
paragraphs: THE CHURCH CANNOT PREACH GRACE BY PRETENDING REPENTANCE IS UNNECESSARY
When “come as you are” quietly becomes “stay as you are,” we have not made the Gospel more compassionate. We have forgotten what Jesus came to save us from.
There is a version of grace that almost everyone can applaud.
It comforts but never confronts.
It forgives but never calls anything sin.
It welcomes the wounded but never asks the rebellious to surrender.
It speaks endlessly about the love of Jesus while becoming strangely uncomfortable with the words Jesus Himself preached:
“Repent.”
And perhaps that is why this conversation matters so much.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is asking God to bless the very thing that is destroying them.
Someone is calling bondage “freedom.”
Someone is repeatedly returning to pornography and telling himself grace means he does not need to fight anymore.
Someone is carrying bitterness into another year because forgiveness feels too costly.
Someone is sleeping beside a person who is not their spouse while convincing themselves that a loving God would never interfere with their happiness.
Someone is hiding dishonesty behind ministry language.
Someone sings worship songs on Sunday while feeding an addiction in secret on Monday.
Someone has learned enough Christian vocabulary to explain grace while using that grace as permission never to change.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that such people have never entered a church.
Perhaps they have.
Perhaps we taught them how to feel accepted without teaching them what Jesus meant when He said:
“Follow Me.”
Grace is not God standing at a distance from our destruction saying, “It doesn’t matter.”
Grace is God entering our destruction in the Person of Jesus Christ, bearing our judgment on a cross, rising from the grave, and calling us out of the tomb with Him.
That difference is everything.
When Jesus began His public proclamation according to Mark 1:15, His message included these words:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek is breathtakingly direct:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
“Repair yourself until God accepts you.”
He did not say, “Become morally impressive, then come back.”
He did not say, “Pay for yesterday with enough good behavior tomorrow.”
The Gospel is not self-salvation.
Jesus announced good news.
Yet the same Jesus who proclaimed good news commanded repentance.

The Greek verb μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite carries the idea of changing one’s mind, but biblical repentance cannot be reduced to merely adopting a different opinion. In Scripture, the changed mind turns the person toward God. Sin is no longer defended as master. The sinner turns toward the One who saves.
That does not mean Christians become instantly flawless.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples misunderstood Jesus repeatedly.
The New Testament never presents Christian maturity as immediate sinlessness.
But there is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin.
One says:
“Jesus, I hate that I keep falling here. Have mercy on me. Help me fight.”
The other says:
“Jesus, I have decided this is no longer something You are permitted to confront.”
Those are not the same posture.
And some of us know exactly which one we have been living.
That is where this article becomes uncomfortable.
Because the easiest person to deceive spiritually is sometimes the person who already knows all the Christian answers.
You know Jesus died for sinners.
You know salvation is by grace.
You know Romans.
You know Ephesians.
You know how to say, “Nobody is perfect.”
All of those truths can be spoken correctly.
And then one terrifying little question remains:
Have you turned toward Christ, or have you merely learned enough about grace to become comfortable hiding from Him?
The Hebrew Scriptures give us another powerful picture.
In Ezekiel 18:30, God calls His people:
שׁוּבוּ וְהָשִׁיבוּ מִכָּל־פִּשְׁעֵיכֶם
shuvu vehashivu mikol-pish'eikhem
The language comes from the Hebrew root שׁוּב — shuv, meaning “turn” or “return.”
That image matters.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Returning.
Coming home.
Sin says, “Keep walking away.”
Shame says, “You have walked too far away to return.”
Grace says:
“Turn around.”
That is why biblical repentance and biblical grace are not enemies.
They meet in the arms of Jesus.
Repentance does not mean cleaning yourself before approaching Christ.
It means abandoning the fantasy that anything other than Christ can save you.
This is why Acts 2 is so striking.
Peter preaches Christ crucified and risen. The people are “pricked in their heart” and ask what they should do.
Peter answers:
Μετανοήσατε
Metanoēsate.
“Repent.”
Then comes the promise of forgiveness and the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Peter did not soften the Gospel by removing repentance.
He preached repentance because forgiveness was actually available.
Think about that.
A doctor who discovers cancer does not demonstrate compassion by hiding the diagnosis.
A firefighter does not love a sleeping family by whispering politely while their house burns.
And the Church does not love sinners by becoming embarrassed to tell them what Jesus came to rescue them from.
We can scream about judgment without love and distort the heart of God.
But we can also whisper about love while refusing to mention judgment, holiness, repentance, or surrender—and distort the Gospel just as surely.
Jesus gives us something infinitely better than either distortion.
Truth full of grace.
Grace full of truth.
A cross where sin is shown to be so serious that the Son of God dies—and sinners are shown to be so deeply loved that the Son of God willingly dies for them.
Look at the cross long enough and two lies become impossible to maintain.
You cannot honestly say:
“My sin does not matter.”
And you cannot honestly say:
“There is no hope left for someone like me.”
Calvary destroys both lies.
Your sin mattered enough for blood to be shed.
And you mattered enough for Christ to willingly shed His.
But we must be precise here.
You are not saved because your repentance is impressive enough.
You are not justified because you cried hard enough.
You are not forgiven because you accumulated enough remorse.
Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9 that salvation is by grace through faith, “not of works.”
Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He bore sin upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
Salvation rests upon Christ.
Even repentance is not a bargaining chip we place on God's counter and exchange for forgiveness.
We come empty-handed.
That is grace.
But empty hands cannot simultaneously cling to the throne of the sin from which Christ is calling us.
That is repentance.
And maybe this is where your heart started beating differently.
Because perhaps there is something you have been defending.
Not struggling with.
Defending.
There is a difference.
Maybe nobody knows.
The deleted messages.
The browser history.
The resentment.
The secret relationship.
The money.
The lies.
The substance you swear you can control.
The jealousy disguised as discernment.
The pride disguised as standards.
The cruelty disguised as “speaking truth.”
The unforgiveness you have rehearsed so many times that bitterness now feels like part of your personality.
You keep asking God for peace while protecting the thing disturbing your peace.
You keep asking Him for freedom while keeping a spare key to the prison.
And Jesus still calls:
“Come.”
Not because the sin is harmless.
Because His mercy is greater.
That is the scandal of grace.
Consider the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Jesus refused to participate in the mob’s self-righteous condemnation.
But He also did not rename adultery as righteousness.
After her accusers departed, Jesus told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Mercy.
Then transformation.
No condemnation from Christ toward the woman standing before Him.
But also no permission to return comfortably to what was destroying her.
This is where modern Christianity sometimes wants to cut Jesus’ sentence in half.
We love:
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
We become nervous around:
“Go, and sin no more.”
But Jesus said both.
Because perfect love does both.
Grace does not merely rescue you from the penalty of sin and then abandon you beneath its domination.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God that brings salvation also teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.
Read that carefully.
Grace teaches us to say no.
The very grace some use as an excuse not to change is described by Scripture as training believers toward godliness.
Real grace has teeth.
Not teeth that devour the repentant sinner.
Teeth that begin breaking the chains around that sinner.
And yes, sometimes transformation is painfully slow.
Sometimes sanctification looks like victory followed by tears, followed by confession, followed by getting up again.
A Christian may stumble terribly.
David did.
Peter did.
The Corinthian church was full of people requiring serious correction.
First John was written to believers and acknowledges the reality of sin while directing them toward confession and Christ our Advocate.
So this is not a message saying:
“Real Christians never fall.”
It is saying:
Real grace does not teach us to call falling freedom.
There is a difference between falling into the mud and building your house there.
There is a difference between needing mercy and demanding permission.
There is a difference between saying, “Father, forgive me,” and saying, “Father, redefine holiness so I never have to surrender.”
Jesus loves us too deeply for the second.
Remember Zacchaeus.
Jesus entered the home of a man despised as a tax collector.
Grace walked through his door before respectable society thought he deserved it.
But after encountering Jesus, Zacchaeus began talking about restitution.
Something changed.
Jesus did not merely become another decoration inside Zacchaeus’s old life.
Christ disrupted it.
That is what grace does.
Not because good works purchase salvation.
They do not.
But because encounters with Jesus produce fruit.
John the Baptist put it sharply in Matthew 3:8:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
Fruit does not create the tree.
Fruit reveals something about the tree.
And that distinction protects us from two cliffs.
Legalism says:
“Change enough and maybe God will love you.”
Cheap grace says:
“God loves you, therefore change is irrelevant.”
The Gospel says:
God loved sinners so profoundly that Christ died for us while we were sinners, and the Christ who saves us now calls us to follow Him.
Come filthy.
Come ashamed.
Come addicted.
Come angry.
Come confused.
Come after another failure.
Come when you have nothing impressive to offer.
But come to Jesus.
Do not come asking Jesus merely to become the chaplain of a life you refuse to surrender.
He is Savior.
He is Lord.
And there is astonishing tenderness in His lordship.
Some people hear “repent” and imagine God screaming, “Get away from Me.”
Biblical repentance announces almost the opposite:
The door home is open. Turn around.
The prodigal son rehearsed his shame while walking home.
He knew he had sinned.
He did not return declaring his rebellion healthy.
He returned confessing it.
And while he was still far away, the father ran.
Do you understand what that means for the person reading this with tears beginning to gather?
You can turn around.
Today.
Not after becoming impressive.
Not after fixing every consequence.
Not after proving yourself worthy.
You were never going to make yourself worthy.
That is why Jesus came.
The cross already tells the truth about your sin.
The empty tomb already tells the truth about His victory.
Stop hiding.
Come home.
Maybe you have spent years believing repentance means God wants to humiliate you.
But repentance is often the moment humiliation ends because pretending ends.
No more double life.
No more defending darkness.
No more exhausting performance.
No more smiling for church while secretly bleeding inside.
You finally say:
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“This is what I became.”
“This is what I keep returning to.”
“I cannot rescue myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
And the Christian Gospel does not answer that confession with:
“Try harder until God tolerates you.”
It points to Christ.
First John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Why “just”?
Because Christian forgiveness is not God pretending evil never happened.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Christ bore sin.
The debt was not waved away as meaningless.
The Savior paid at immeasurable cost.
This is why Romans 2:4 says that God's kindness leads toward repentance.
Not away from it.
Toward it.
Grace is not the cancellation of repentance.
Grace makes repentance possible without despair.
You can confess because there is mercy.
You can surrender because there is a Savior.
You can stop pretending because Jesus already knows.
You can come out of hiding because the One waiting for you bears scars.
So perhaps the question is no longer whether churches should preach repentance.
Perhaps the question is:
How could we preach the cross faithfully without it?
What exactly did Jesus die to save us from if sin is something we must never confront?
Why speak about forgiveness if there is nothing requiring forgiveness?
Why celebrate redemption if captivity is merely another lifestyle?
Why proclaim resurrection if nobody needs to come out of a grave?
The Gospel is glorious precisely because our condition was desperate and Christ was sufficient.
We were not slightly inconvenienced.
We needed salvation.
And Jesus saves.
This message must therefore never become ammunition for self-righteous Christians who enjoy identifying everybody else’s sins.
Before pointing across the room, look at your own heart.
Repentance begins here.
With me.
With you.
The proud need repentance.
The gossip needs repentance.
The pastor needs repentance.
The person addicted to pornography needs repentance.
The religious hypocrite needs repentance.
The greedy need repentance.
The sexually immoral need repentance.
The unforgiving need repentance.
The self-righteous person condemning everyone else needs repentance.
The person writing Christian articles needs repentance.
Nobody stands at the foot of the cross as the impressive one.
We stand there as people whose only boast is Jesus Christ.
So when the Church preaches repentance, it should never sound like superior people yelling at inferior people.
It should sound like rescued people shouting toward people still trapped in the fire:
“There is a way out. His name is Jesus.”
Be honest.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Somebody reading your words may discover they are not the only believer fighting that battle.
And somebody else may pray for you tonight.
If this message made you think of one person immediately, do not merely think about them.
It may be where hope begins.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday’s convictions feel distant tomorrow.
Return to it when you are tempted to rename what God is asking you to surrender.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the exhausted believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Not because Gospel Warrior can save anybody.
We cannot.
Jesus Christ saves.
This ministry exists to keep pointing toward Him.
It does not make you more spiritual, more forgiven, or more loved by God. Salvation cannot be bought, and supporting a Christian ministry should never be confused with supporting the Gospel itself.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with your resources, one practical expression of Christian stewardship can be voluntarily supporting work that helps spread His Word. Sharing this article publicly is another.
Do not leave this article merely supporting a ministry while refusing to surrender your heart to Christ.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
The merchandise cannot save you.
The library cannot save you.
Religion cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your tears cannot save you.
Your promises to “do better” cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Believe the Gospel.
And when you fall, do not run away from the One whose blood purchased forgiveness.
Run toward Him.
The Church does not need less grace.
We need grace in all its breathtaking biblical fullness.
Grace that welcomes the prodigal.
Grace that forgives the adulterer.
Grace that restores the failure.
Grace that confronts the hypocrite.
Grace that humbles the proud.
Grace that cleanses the guilty.
Grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace that finds sinners exactly where they are—
but loves them far too much to pretend captivity is freedom.
That is the scandal.
Holy God.
Guilty sinners.
A crucified Savior.
An empty grave.
Mercy offered to people who could never earn it.
And a voice still calling through the centuries:
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Me.
Maybe you came into this article afraid that repentance meant Jesus was finished with you.
Perhaps you can finally see the opposite.
He is calling you to turn because He is not finished with you yet.
Then close the screen for a moment.
Forget the comments.
Forget the shares.
Forget the algorithm.
Forget Gospel Warrior.
And answer the question that matters when nobody else can hear you:
What is Jesus asking you to stop defending and finally surrender?
Because the most dangerous prison may not be the sin you keep falling into.
It may be the sin you have finally stopped wanting freedom from.
